utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Two short preliminary matters. The first deals with P580. In the current translation, paragraph 1 doesn't have a full text in English. The Prosecution has uploaded a revised translation under doc ID 0529-3107-1-ET. As always, Mr. Lukic, the Defence has an opportunity to revisit the matter within the next 48 hours, or you could perhaps, if there is any need to do that, through an e-mail. But meanwhile, I already instruct to replace the existing translation of P580 with the revised version, uploaded under the doc ID I mentioned a minute ago. Then the Chamber understands that the Prosecution would like to give a short statement in relation to D735 MFI'd and D736 MFI'd. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And good morning. Regarding Exhibits D735 and D736, marked for identification, the Trial Chamber requested any additional submissions from the Prosecution by today's date. D735 is the statement of Witness Nedjo Vlaski, as redacted by the Defence. D736 is an 18-page proofing note, which we understand is primarily to provide Mr. Vlaski's basis for knowledge for some of the paragraphs in the statement where the basis of knowledge was unclear. We maintain our position that the witness's basis for knowledge is unclear as in certain paragraphs in D735, the statement, which were identified in our response to the Defence 92 ter motion for Mr. Vlaski. The probative value of the other paragraphs we also maintain are limited. However, after a review of the witness's examination, we believe that the Trial Chamber is in a position to properly assess the weight, if any, to be given to Mr. Vlaski's statement and we will not further litigate the matter. Similarly, we understand that D736, the proofing note, was used based on the circumstances unique to Vlaski's evidence. The Prosecution at the time was concerned about the length of the proofing note and the possibility of this becoming practice in the case. While we would maintain this concern, this instance appears to be an exception. On the understanding that the tendering of the proofing note was triggered by those unique circumstances, we will also not further seek to litigate this issue. On the basis of this, the Prosecution withdraws its objections to the admission of D735 and D736, marked for identification. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber. Could you refresh my memory as to whether the witness attested to the proofing note?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: He did. It was my recollection that he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Under those circumstances, nothing opposes admission of D735 and D736. Both are therefore admitted. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness, which, if I understand well, would be Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. The witness, Mr. Simic, has been added to your 65 ter list, and the Chamber approved that, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Reasons still to be given. We'll give them in due course. Good morning, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Simic. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: My apologies for forgetting to raise this just before the witness came in, but this witness was admonished pursuant to Rule 90(E) in the previous proceedings, and we believe, based on his evidence and the content of even his statement and his position, that it would be proper to do so before he testifies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. We have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, before we start hearing your evidence, I would like to inform you about the content of Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I'll read it to you. "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." If you think that a truthful answer to one of the questions might tend to incriminate yourself, you may address me and ask to be relieved from answering that question. You'll now first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find Mr. Stojanovic to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please slowly tell us your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Savo Simic is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, have you given a written statement to the Defence team of Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up in e-court 1D03977.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the last page. Mr. Simic, you see the screen before you. You see the last page of the document. Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's my signature. And the date is 4 November 2012.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the date in the left bottom corner of the document, is it in your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, in the proofing before you appeared in the courtroom today, did you tell me that you wanted to make a few clarifications and corrections to your statement?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will quickly go through them and you will just confirm, please, if that is exactly what you told me. In paragraph 2 of your statement, in line 3, instead of the words "in the 49th Mechanised Brigade of the JNA," you told me it would be more correct to write "in the 134th Artillery Division of the multiple rocket launchers Plamen, flame [as interpreted]." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the same paragraph number 2, in line 11, instead of the word "independent," there should be "self-propelled." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 6 of your statement, line 2, you indicated it would be correct to replace the word "motorised" by "mechanised." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I am a bit confused. In the statement, I read in line 2 "the 49th Mechanised Brigade." What shall be changed there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it, looking at the original text, that the B/C/S says "motorised" and that it is already translated, right or wrong, with "mechanised"?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Motorised, that's correct, Your Honour. Just to avoid confusion. Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 9 of your statement, in line 2, the word "artillery pieces" should be replaced by "units," "artillery units." And in line 1 behind the word "directly" the word "professionally" or "technically" should be inserted. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm again somewhat puzzled. Line 2, where you said "artillery pieces" should be replaced by "artillery units." In the translation, I only see "the following weapons were there ..." Or is it "As for the artillery under my..." command.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, this particular word, "orudja," means "artillery weapons."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has said, Your Honours, that he had under his control not weapons but units. He wants the word "weapons" to be replaced by "units" in order to make it more correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear by now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've already confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 21 of your statement, you've indicated that in the first sentence the words "when I took up my duties of desk officer in the artillery organ of the SRK command" should be deleted. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in paragraph 23 of your statement, in the sixth passage, you noticed a place name that is incorrectly written, and you said that the word "Vukovici" should be replaced by "Vojkovici." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And for precision's sake, in items 12, 17, 27, and 28, instead of the acronym or abbreviation "1st Sntbr," the letter T should be deleted. The correct acronym for your unit was 1st Smbr. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now after making these corrections and after giving a solemn declaration in the courtroom today, if I were to ask you the same questions as when you were giving the statement, would you give us identical answers?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would repeat exactly the same answers as recorded in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do these answers reflect your best knowledge and recollection of the events you were asked about?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should like to tender the witness statement of Savo Simic under the number 1D03977.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, paragraph 21 of statement, you deleted, more or less, the time-frame - that is, "When I became an officer in the SRK artillery command or the desk officer." Would you like to replace that by any other time-frame or is it just that the witness saw it for the first time although we do not know when?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, because it's quite clear from the text that follows which duties he had in the second half of 1994. The words that were deleted could only create confusion and that's why the witness wanted them out, because it's quite clear from the statement where he was and what his responsibilities were in the second half of 1994 in paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And indeed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There remains still a time-frame in paragraph 21. Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number would be D1062.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should also like to tender the map marked by the witness, 65 ter 1D03978, as a document accompanying the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number would be D1063.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. If you've any further questions to the witness, but perhaps after you have read the summary of his statement, you may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Savo Simic was born in 1959 and he's a professional military man, currently retired, in the rank of colonel. When the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he was in Sarajevo serving as a JNA officer; i.e., commander of the multiple rocket launcher Plamen battery. During the war, he carried out the duties of chief of artillery in the 1st Sarajevo Brigade of the VRS, then commander of the 4th Mixed Anti-Armour Artillery Regiment of the SRK, and finally desk officer in the artillery organ of the SRK command. In his statement, he describes the situation in the JNA units on the eve of the war, the fact that JNA professional officers of non-Serb origin were leaving the JNA. He speaks about the incidents of desertion, the deployment of JNA units, and the activities taken to prevent the blockade of these units. He speaks in detail about the types and the number of artillery weapons that were in his unit's possession and the deployment of these weapons. He states that the principal task of the SRK was to protect ethnic Serb sectors in Sarajevo and its environs and to confront the forces of the BH Army that were striving to break out of the city which would have had a great impact on other front lines and the entire course of the war. He is familiar with the firing positions of the BH Army mortars in the city of Sarajevo and on Mount Igman, and it is his opinion that they very skillfully used the city to deploy their artillery inside parks, on top of buildings, or mounted on vehicles. In the artillery positions of his brigade, there was UNPROFOR presence and the UNPROFOR observers recorded every firing, the targets, and also the reasons why a specific object was targeted. He himself and his unit never intended to cause civilian casualties or to terrorise civilians in Sarajevo. He describes his experience with modified air bombs and their precision, and he enumerates the military targets of the BH Army located in civilian areas as well as the offensives launched by the BH Army targeting the SRK. In conclusion, he presents his own position as a professional artillery officer on individual incidents cited in the indictment and related to Sarajevo. That was the short summary of this witness's statement, and I would now like, Your Honours, to ask a few questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D1062, could we please have that and could we focus on paragraphs 9 and 10 of the statement. D1062.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, in paragraph 9 you speak about artillery that was under your direct professional command from the 29th of May, 1992, and you enumerate all of that. However, for us who are not trained in the field of artillery weaponry, there is something that remains unclear and I would like you to state something for the record: When you say "three howitzer batteries," could you please tell us how many howitzers that involves?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: In each battery I had six pieces, so it is a total of 18 artillery pieces in these howitzer batteries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This number of six weapons, does it also refer to 122-millimetre self-propelled howitzer batteries? You call them Gvozdika here.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are special batteries and they also had six pieces per battery. So the total is 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How many VBR multiple rocket launchers did VBR batteries have?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: The battery of 128-millimetre Plamen multiple rocket launchers had a total of four weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I will conclude with one final question: How many weapons did two 120-millimetre mortar batteries have?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Six per battery. That is the general rule and that was the case in my own unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 10 of your statement, you say that already in June 1992 from the area of Sarajevo certain artillery pieces left, one went to the area of Han Pijesak and another one in the direction of Milici, on orders from the Main Staff. This number of artillery pieces from paragraph 9, did it include these two batteries that had left you or did you have all these weapons even without them?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: These units that at the beginning and end of June 1992 were sent to Han Pijesak and Milici were from the units mentioned in paragraph 9. So out of the three howitzer batteries mentioned here, D100-millimetre, D30, one left, and towards the end of June, one 122-millimetre self-propelled Gvozdika howitzer battery left, so it included six weapons and also one squad of 128-millimetre Plamen multiple rocket launchers. So these are not any kind of additional units. These are the units that I mentioned in paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Until the end of your involvement in this unit, the 1st Sarajevo Brigade, did any other weapons go to some other unit or were some of those weapons deployed elsewhere outside Sarajevo? Some of these weapons mentioned in paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. In February, March, on orders from the Main Staff, the second self-propelled Gvozdika howitzer battery left, and it became part of the 1st Motorised Guards Brigade. So it was February or March. So, that is to say, the order came before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we please have a time-frame, year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could you elicit a time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, we would just like to ask you when it was that this happened? When did this battery go to the Guards Brigade on orders from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: The end of February. And its transfer to the 1st Guards Brigade was completed in March 1993. Since conditions were difficult then, the snow was deep, and - how do I put this - the transfer of the unit could not take place in one go. The conditions were very difficult. So this went on for a few days. So end of February, beginning of March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, may I just briefly consult the General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's done at a nonaudible volume, you may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, again I can hear you and so everyone else can. Mr. Stojanovic, just --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a matter totally unrelated to the questioning of the witness at this moment. Earlier today we admitted D736, that is admitted under seal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question about these characteristics of the weapons. When you mentioned multiple rocket launchers, VBR, you said that a battery has four weapons.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: I am saying that my battery had four weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you how many barrels one weapon had, this VBR Plamen? How many could be fired at the same time?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: 128 millimetres, and there were three regimes of firing: A burst of gun-fire, there could have been a burst of gun-fire or individual, three regiments from .2, .4, .6 seconds, one rocket. So if the regime is 0.2 seconds, then all three could be fired. If it was 04, 0.4 seconds, in 24 seconds, all 36 would be fired. And it's 0.6 seconds, then 18.6 seconds, all 32 rockets would be fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, first of all, I'd like to invite you to slow down. It's still not entirely clear how many barrels had every system apart from the -- how they were fired. Again, I can hear Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, let's -- Take off your earphones, Mr. Mladic, and whisper. Could you tell us how many barrels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, sir, one weapon, a multiple rocket launcher, had 32 barrels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you in a position to fire an entire salvo at one point in time from a multiple rocket launcher?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: I never had the opportunity of firing a full salvo, that is to say, with all the weapons, because I didn't have enough ammunition, I didn't have such targets to engage either, so that I could use all that ammunition which I had to save anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 16, my last question. Let us focus on paragraph 16, D1062. I had some information and data about the disposition of the 1st Corps forces. Could you please explain this to the Trial Chamber so that we do not leave it on this very general phrase, "I had some information ..." Specifically, where did you get specific information about these elements; that is to say, concerning the disposition of the 1st Corps forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: From the very beginning of combat, as soon as the war broke out in Sarajevo, I organised observation points at dominant features around Sarajevo, which is in accordance with the rules. There were trained officers there and also trained operators. In addition to instruments for reconnaissance and for observation - that is to say, in view of the area held by the enemy - they also had established contacts and communications with the artillery battalion command and their own batteries. So most of the information I got was by direct observation of enemy forces. I also had some forward observation posts as required by combat as it evolved. So that is one way in which information is gathered. As enemy forces are observed directly. Also, I received intelligence from the intelligence organ of the corps command. So I received information in that way about the deployment of enemy forces, and then I would verify that myself. I would observe it from the observation point to see whether this information is valid, correct, and so on. I would attain information in other ways as well. For example, if there were exchanges of population or if some people fled, I spoke to some of these people, and I was primarily interested in the firing positions of the Muslim army in Sarajevo, their observation points, the town command, et cetera. So whatever information they were able to provide, and they were in a position to provide quite a bit, then they talked about the fortification of observation points, and then they walked around and they saw some things and they gave me information of that nature. I verified such information as well. So I checked, verified that. I didn't engage any targets just like that. I asked my observers to make sure that they would see where the command post is, where the firing positions were among the enemy forces in the area of Sarajevo or anywhere else outside Sarajevo. So these were mainly the sources from which I obtained my information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at this point in time, we have no further questions for Mr. Simic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Before I give an opportunity to Mr. Weber to start his cross-examination, I would have one question, Witness. It relates to paragraph 26 of your statement and deals with incidents G-5 and G-6. You're telling us there that according to the finds of the BH police, 82-millimetre mortar shells had been fired from Serbian firing positions. You say: "My opinion about these incidents is that the shells were fired from the Butmir sector from positions under the control of the Muslim forces." Now, it's clear that you disagree, but the reasons for this disagreement are not set out there in what respect you think the BH police made mistakes or did not properly analyse. Could you give us the reasons why you disagree with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, 82-millimetre mortars are support weapons for battalions, and it is battalion commanders that control their use. From a professional point of view, as I'm a professional artilleryman, I came to the conclusion that it was not possible to establish exactly from which position the mentioned shell was fired from the 82-millimetre mortar. For example, it says that it was fired from Nedzarici. And in the direction of Nedzarici, there is also Butmir, and we established that they had firing positions there, where the UPI Institute was. I mean, I'm just saying here that it is not possible to establish that it is exactly from Serb positions. Now, whether there was a detailed investigation on the basis of the angle of descent, the azimuth, whether that was all done very precisely, I really don't know. But I assume, as an artillery officer, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a second. If I understand you well, you're saying they could have been fired from Butmir as well, just as they could have been fired from Serb positions? Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said there is one direction of firing but the distance had to be established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's not what your statement says. Your statement says that it's your opinion that they were fired from Butmir, not that they could have been fired from Butmir as well. But that's now clear to me. There is another matter. You said: I don't know what they measured, azimuth, angle of descent, et cetera, et cetera. Have you seen the reports in which the BH police concluded that they were fired from Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read some reports, but -- I mean, as far as I understood things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you read these reports about G-5 and G-6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did I see these reports about G-5 and G-6? Those incidents? Did I read them? Yes, I read them. And as far as I understood these reports, it was not exactly established and that the azimuths were not measured properly, that the distance of firing was not established, and that this cannot be established with any precision. And it is a very small distance, Nedzarici and the place where the shell fell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because a minute ago you said, and I'll literally quote what you said: "Now, whether there was a detailed investigation on the basis of the angle of descent, the azimuth, whether that was all done very precisely, I really don't know." That suggests that you have not studied those reports because you say I don't know what they did and what was the basis for their conclusions. I'm a bit puzzled by you now telling me that you did read the reports. Do you have an explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we haven't understood each other, Judge, sir, well, in detail. As far as I understood what I read, it was not done professionally. There were certain deviations, there were different interpretations. I think there were some two commissions there and there was a discrepancy, and this leads me to the conclusion that this was not done fully as it should have been done, to measure the exact azimuth, the angle of descent and -- actually, it is not sufficient just to establish the direction of firing. It is also important to establish the distance in order to see where it was that the shell was fired from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when you said I don't know whether that was all done and what they took into account, you say you did look at that and you think that their conclusions are wrong on the basis of what you read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on the basis of what I read. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Weber. You find Mr. Weber to your right. Mr. Weber is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, in July 1993 and January 1994, you were not [realtime transcript read in error: "Now"] assigned to the Ilidza Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. In July 1993 and January 1994, I was within the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You were not assigned or giving orders to the artillery units of the Ilidza Brigade at the school of -- the Faculty of Theology building or near the Nedzarici barracks, correct, on those months?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, could you have a look at the transcript. Page 20, line 2. I think I heard instead of the word "now" I heard the word "not." Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Not. I believe I said "not assigned."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what my impression was as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Moving on to some other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You were a member of the 49th JNA Mechanised Brigade prior to May 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The 49th Mechanised Brigade was a part of the 4th Corps of the JNA; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The headquarters of the 49th Mechanised Brigade was in the area of Lukavica; do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the area of Lukavica, in the Slavisa Vajner Cica barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's the same barracks that the brigade stayed in when it was renamed the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: When the brigade was renamed the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, it was already relocated from the barracks and it was outside. It was at the positions, and the command post was in the area of Pavlovac, close to the barracks but not in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P6534 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Colonel Simic, this is a 4th Corps order dated 17th May 1992, concerning the changes in titles of units. Directing your attention to item 2 on this list, which indicates the 49th Mbr, is receiving the title 1st Sarajevo Brigade. Your brigade was renamed the 1st Sarajevo Brigade in May 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to item 1, this occurred at the same time that the 4th Corps was renamed the Sarajevo Romanija Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With this re-designation, you became a member of the Army of Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: As a member of the artillery units of the 49th Brigade and then the 1st Smbr, your artillery units communicated with reconnaissance and sabotage or DIO units; correct? They were another means of you obtaining information?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: I established observation posts. That is what artillery rules say anyway. So in addition to firing positions, every unit has to have observation points. You cannot target without correcting fire from observation posts. So I established observation posts, and I had observers, I had scouts, and I received information about the enemy. Also, I received information from other units. They would provide information to me. As regards units that I could not observe for my own observations posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, please listen to my questions carefully. I understand what you're saying. My question was intended to be more directed towards you communicated with reconnaissance and sabotage units, known as DIO units; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: I didn't know any kind of units for sabotage. I'm not familiar with such units. I did communicate with my own units and the units of the superior command, of course with the superior command. Those are the observation posts that I communicated with. And also with neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In 1991 and the first half of 1992, reserve forces responded to call-ups and joined the 49th Mechanised Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: At the summons from the command of the mechanised brigade, first of all, training was conducted for critical specialties such as commanders of units, topographers, and gunners - gunners were the most critical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question was whether reserve forces responded to call-ups and joined the 49th Mechanised Brigade. Did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just about to say that. Only Serbs responded to the call-ups to the brigade, whereas as of 1991 Slovenes and Croats did not go to the army and later on we were unable to call them up even as reserves, because only Serbs responded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I also seek clarification of one of your previous answers. You were asked about communication with sabotage and reconnaissance units known as DIO units. You said there were no sabotage units. But was there any reconnaissance units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were reconnaissance units within the brigade. And I said I received information from all units, including them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, following up on your last question, if the Prosecution could have 65 ter 32637 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I said please proceed but I think I should have said let's take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we take a break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back after the break. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I invite the parties also to look at page 21, line 6, 7, although the line numbers are sometimes slightly different, where the witness said, talking about the brigade: "The command post was close to the barracks but in the barracks." I think it was "but not in the barracks." But perhaps could we at any point in time verify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Simic. You may proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. On the screen, for the record, we have 65 ter 32637.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Colonel Simic, I'd like to direct your attention to this document. It is a 4th Corps intelligence sector report dated 13 January 1992 from the chief of intelligence sector, Milisav Petrovic. In section a of this report, it indicates that the corps has five reconnaissance companies, two of these companies are in the 10th and 49th Brigades. In section b it then -- towards the second half of the doc -- page before you, it lists a bunch of material needed for the companies. As you see a little further down in section b, which is probably towards the bottom-third of the page before you, it lists a bunch of material needed for the companies. One of the items were "silencers for automatic rifle, sniper rifle, and API for all of our reconnaissance companies." Sir, the reconnaissance units of your brigade possessed these types of rifles; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I really don't know what they had at their disposal, especially since I was commander of a battery at that time. I don't know what they had. I don't know what they had and what they missed. I could not answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders the document into evidence, 65 ter 32637.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document receives number P7398.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I now want to return to what we were discussing in terms of the individuals who joined the 49th Brigade in 1991 and early 1992. There were also volunteers who joined the brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in the early days of combat, mainly conscripts and volunteers filled the units. It was difficult to carry out the mobilisation. Officers were mobilised on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, you've answered my question. If you could just -- I will go through it step by step. There is no need to explain. And just so I know, the JNA 4th Corps provided these individuals who were called up, and volunteers, they provided them with weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: I mean volunteers from the population of surrounding villages, Lukavica, Tilava. I mean, these volunteers responded of their own will because there was no state of war declared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you have not listened to the question, apparently, because the question was not whether they -- where they came from. The question was whether they were provided with weapons. Were they or were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they received weapons, they were trained, and they got weapons in the unit where they were assigned within the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Since you've mentioned the ethnic makeup of the individuals who joined, I'd like to show you 65 ter 19789a.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please have page 10 of the B/C/S original and page 15 of the English translation. For the record, coming up are the attachments referenced in Exhibit P1967. There are a total of seven attachments mentioned in that other exhibit and these are the seven attachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Colonel Simic, this is Colonel Aleksa Krsmanovic's report which was delivered during a 15 November 1992 consultation on the military political situation in the SRK zone of responsibility. Section 1 remits to the manning of officers and soldiers as of November 1992, as I understand it. It indicates units were manned with active and reserve officers, non-commissioned officers, civilians working in the army, soldiers under contract, military conscripts, soldiers doing their national service in the RS, and by many patriots and patriotically inclined people. If you could look a little then further down, he then -- Colonel Krsmanovic states that the characteristics of the manning in the SRK as: "Mono-ethnic (99.8 per cent Serbs, 0.02 per cent the rest)." He then indicates the age structure as -- the average age is 36 years of age. This is consistent with the unit that you were in, correct, your brigade?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, the ethnic structure is correct. I don't know the exact percentage, but in the early days of the war, in my unit I also had some Muslim soldiers and Croat soldiers. Those who were doing their regular military service and were sent from Serbia and Montenegro. All the way up to 19 May 1992, when the JNA withdrew from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that this is a large upload. We can do -- at this time I'd suggest either one of two things: Either mark for identification the entire document, which we do intend to use later; or I'd be happy to excerpt just Colonel Krsmanovic's portion now and seek that admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you not say these are annexes to already an existing --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- exhibit, P967?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: They are, but the annexes are not admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In general, we believe that it would be helpful for an understanding of the other exhibit too, to have these annexes, but I've only used a small portion right now so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's the total size of the document, if you would ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There's seven annexes. I believe it's over 20 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it really is 20 pages, then there is no problem in having it all in. But if it would be considerably more, then you would be invited to extract.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's 18 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 18 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. You may upload it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It is uploaded. Then we tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 19789a receives number P7399.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. And I did understand that you're using other portions later as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We do intend to, and we've also used P1967 on a number of occasions. So the materials do interrelate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: From May 1992 [realtime transcript read in error: "1990"] until May 1994, you were the chief of the artillery in the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. In this capacity, did you oversee the use of all artillery and mortars in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, can you just check. You said from May 19...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: My understanding is from his statement, from May 1992 until May 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Because you are recorded as saying "May 1990."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, from May 1992 to May 1994, I was chief of artillery in the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. The chief of artillery is a professional organ in the command of the brigade. So technically I was responsible for the readiness and the level of training of units and their fitness for carrying out tasks. I was not the commander of these units. I was the professional supervisor of these units that I named in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Please listen to my question carefully. I wanted to know did you oversee the use, so the actual use, of artillery and mortars in the 1st Smbr.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I oversaw the use of these units. The brigade artillery group. Those are the units I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The question was not related to the unit but if you -- the use of all artillery and mortars in the brigade. Did you oversee that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I oversaw the use of the two mortar batteries that I indicated that made up the brigade artillery group. I also supervised the howitzer batteries, 122-millimetres, while they were in the brigade and the multiple rocket launchers, but I oversaw the level of training and the fitness for combat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This was not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but as for the other 122-millimetre batteries, I did not supervisor them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be very helpful if you would just listen to the question and answer the question which was put to you. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This Chamber has received evidence of the various artillery and mortars in the Smbr. Do I understand from your question -- or your answer that you did not oversee the use of all artillery and mortars in the brigade, only certain pieces?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: I can only tell you again. I oversaw the artillery units that I named in my statement. The ones that made up the brigade artillery group. I only had supervision over these units. No other groups. I don't know if anything else existed. I know of nothing else. I know only 122-millimetre mortars. I did not supervise their use.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your brigade commander was Veljko Stojanovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During your time in the 1st Smbr, you provided proposals on the use of artillery to the brigade commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. While I was chief of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Dusan Skrbo [sic] was one of your subordinates; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Dusan Skrba was subordinated to me professionally, not along the chain of command. Along the chain of command, he was directly answerable to the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 32640 for the witness, page 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Colonel Simic, at various points today, just to actually attempt to save us some time, I am going to call up portions of your testimony in the Karadzic case where you discuss different matters. I will read you these portions, I will try to do it slowly, and then afterwards I will have questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document is not released in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you for letting us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just so we know, do you understand the English language?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On this part, I'm going to start on line 11. In the Karadzic case, you are asked: "Let me follow up on some of those questions, Colonel Simic. As chief of artillery in the 1st Mechanised Brigade, what were your general responsibilities? I know you already alluded to some of them in your previous answer, but I'd like to know your formal responsibilities as chief of artillery." Your answer was: "First and foremost, I was supposed to take care of the professional training of the unit for combat tasks. I was not in charge of discipline. It was the battalion commander who was in charge of that and his subordinated commanders were -- reported to him on that. If there was any free time and there was no combat, I organised training so that my unit members were always active, they were always involved in training unless there was combat going on. My other tasks were to inform the brigade commander about the professional capabilities of the unit, the problems of logistics support - if there were any - in terms of artillery so as to make sure that the unit was at all times capable of performing its tasks. When it come to issues of morale, discipline, and the situation in the unit, it was the commander of the battalion who was in charge of that and he was the one who reported on those issues. That would be in a nutshell. And, moreover, in the brigade command I also provided my input on the use of artillery; i.e., I provided my proposal to the brigade commander. And the brigade commander at the end of the day decided whether to accept my proposals or not, or perhaps he had his own suggestions and he would issue orders as to how to place the artillery, how to deploy the assets. And then the orders were carried out. "If a combat order was being drafted, I provided my input for the artillery use, both verbally and graphically, using a map." You were then asked: "And based on that input, assuming it was accepted, it would then be the commander who would issue the order to the subordinate units to the -- for artillery use?" You answered: "Correct." Do you stand by this previous testimony regarding your responsibilities in the 1st Smbr?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. I stand by it. But I would only like to add that it's not a battalion commander but the artillery battalion. You mentioned several times "battalion," but when we talk about artillery battalions, another word in Serbian is used and it sounds "divizija" -- "divizion." "Divizion."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So what you were discussing in that answer was the mixed artillery division of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Correct. Because he was in charge of the brigade artillery group.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, there were two artillery regiments that were directly subordinated to the corps command; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There was the 4th Mixed Anti-Armour Artillery Regiment, which we see in your statement you commanded, and there was also the 4th Mixed Artillery Regiment; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The commander of the 4th MAP, or mixed artillery regiment, was Colonel Radislav Cvetkovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you tell us just who was the previous commander of the 4th Mixed Anti-Armour Artillery Regiment, which is the one you commanded from May 1994 until April 1995? Who was your predecessor?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: The way you put it, May 1994, I was there in May 1994 to May or April 1995, and Bartula, Jovan, Colonel Jovan Bartula served in my position until May 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: As the commander of this regiment, you were directly subordinate to the corps commander, initially General Galic and then General Milosevic; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You also received input on your activities from the SRK chief of artillery as part of this regiment; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The SRK chief of artillery at that time was Tadija Manojlovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: As part of this corps artillery regiment, you sent your reports directly to the corps commander; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I sent reports to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You would also report along your professional lines to Colonel Manojlovic; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: When some technical report was needed, I sent it to Colonel Manojlovic. I don't remember. There were too many of them. For the most part, we simply met and resolved things on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: From April 1995 until the end of the war, you indicate that you were assistant to the chief of artillery in the SRK command. Colonel Manojlovic was your immediate superior; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution now go to page 22 of the transcript which is on the screen before us still.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is the portion of the Karadzic testimony where you described your role in the SRK command. I'm going to start on line 8. What was asked of you was: "I indicated I wanted to now focus on the third role that you identified in your statement and that was, as indicated in the statement, from April 1995 until the end of the war when you were - it says in your statement - a desk officer in the SRK command artillery organ. What were your responsibilities as -- in this position?" Your answer: "I was assistant commander of artillery. I was his desk officer and I carried out his orders and his tasks concerning artillery." Next question. "And what did that involve in terms of your -- both your daily role in either receiving information from subordinate units, drafting plans, and so on? And then I want to ask you after that what it involved in terms of specific operations that were envisioned or carried out?" Your answer, which finishes at the end on the next page, was: "Together with the chief of artillery, I worked on the plan of use of artillery. The chief of artillery made proposals; I assisted him. He would draw the plan of action on the map. And pursuant to the order of the corps commander, we would do excerpts from that plan. That's when it came to combat. And pursuant to the orders of the chief of artillery, if he would send me to one of the corps units, I would go, inspect, and extend assistance if I encountered any problems. I carried out his tasks and orders in that sense." Do you stand by this previous testimony regarding your role in the SRK command?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31139.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is an order dated 12 August 1995 from the personnel administration of the VJ General Staff related to appointments from the 30th Personnel Centre. This document mentions multiple people, such as Marko Lugonja, who we see on the first page. It later mentions individuals like Milorad Sehovac and Milorad Bukova, among others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 8 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the middle of the page before you and at the bottom of the page of the translation, at number 13 on this list we see that your name appears. You and other senior members of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps were assigned to the VRS through the 30th Personnel Centre of the Yugoslav Army, the VJ; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 31139 receives number P7400.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7400 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: While you were in the 1st Smbr -- I actually want to change topics a little bit with you. While you were in the 1st Smbr, orders were provided to subordinate units in both writing and orally; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The orders conveyed to the brigade's units came through the chain of command from the corps command; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Towards the brigade command and then further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you were an artillery commander, the artillery and mortars under your command could not be used without your approval; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: You mean the chief of artillery. I was not the commander. I was the chief of artillery in the brigade, if that's the period you're referring to. Without my knowledge, it was not used if I was there. So I was familiarised with that. The commander of the artillery battalion could decide to use mortars and other weapons from his artillery battalion on orders from the commander of the regiment, and then if I'm not there, then I'm not informed. But if I was at the command post of the brigade, then I was certainly informed, or if I was in the corps, so I was informed about what was happening; that is to say, when artillery was used. It wasn't that I issued orders as to whether it would be used or not but I was made aware of this. I was told that it would be used. So I was following the situation in the unit, and I took that into account, paid attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do I understand from your answer then that the artillery mortars could not be used without the approval of the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: It depended on the situation. If combat operations were such that fire had to be opened immediately, then the artillery battalion commander could -- actually, if the objective was revealed and if there was an attack at the front line, then there had to be immediate reaction. And while the order to open fire at enemy targets was being issued, the commander is informed. So it depended on the situation. But certainly the commander could not determine who would fire when. I mean, that's what he had the commander of the artillery battalion for, and he was responsible for the use of artillery, and he could, without his order, if it has to do with an immediate danger in terms of the combat disposition of our own forces, he could act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I again urge you to slow down when speaking, otherwise some of your words would be lost for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Aside from that situation, if there are orders that the artillery or mortars would be fired, those orders would have to be issued by the brigade commander; correct? It would have to come through him. That's how I understood your previous evidence.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you the brigade commander would approve the use; for example, if combat operations were being planned, then one acts in accordance with the plan of activity. However, if some of the battalion commanders informed the commander of the brigade about danger - namely, that his position was under threat - then the brigade commander is going to order the opening of fire; rather, giving support to the area of responsibility of the commander of that unit. However, there can be a situation when the battalion commander could call us directly and inform us along parallel lines, and we would open fire without waiting for the approval of the brigade commander, if the position is in danger, and if that is confirmed by our own observers from the observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Large-calibre artillery and mortars were valued assets in the SRK; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Valued assets for supporting infantry units, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The use of large-calibre weaponry was controlled through orders from the SRK command; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: The command of the SRK controlled through their orders the use of weaponry, units, so as not to have fire opened unnecessarily, to observe targets, to engage targets, that's it. If we were to ask approval from the brigade commander and then the commander of the corps and the Main Staff, then we wouldn't open fire for an hour or whatever. But there is reporting, subsequently, and everybody in the chain is made aware of the opening of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, we'll go through it. If you could answer my questions as closely to what I ask as possible, that'd be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 32633 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is an order dated 31 October 1992 from Deputy Commander Dragan Marcetic of the SRK command. The order is sent to all units of the SRK. It's a very short order. It states: "As of 1.11.1992 and until further notice, the use of weaponry of a calibre higher than 12.7 millimetres is strictly forbidden without the approval of the Corps commander or his deputy." This is how the SRK command controlled the use of weapons over 12.7 millimetres in calibre; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: This probably pertains to a cease-fire that had been agreed upon. And, in such situations, the corps commander sends such an order forbidding the use without his approval. So such orders were obeyed, we never violated the cease-fire. Our units were never the first to violate a cease-fire. We only responded if we were attacked at the front line, and I think that this pertains to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this will last very long and actually I'll be worried about getting you home tomorrow. If you could please listen to my questions carefully, I -- This document says nothing about a cease-fire; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Really, from the document, you cannot see what it pertains to, but the corps commander could not control the use of fire --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So, sir, there is no need to add things. My question was just very simple about this being an example of something.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 32633 receives number P7401.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When oral orders to fire targets were conveyed to subordinate units, the SRK used coded language and coded tables; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Code-names and such-like was used in conveying such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 32536 for the witness. I'll be going directly to page 7 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The last document which was admitted received P7401.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I just want to go through an example of this coded language and tables. This is an SRK table of signals and targets. We see that there are codes for the periods in the month and for the name of some of the SRK units. We then see that there are designations beginning with the letter C. These designations, which are -- for example, C-30 and then so forth, those are the coded locations of targets; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it seems to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we please have the next page in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We then see that there's instructions for the number of salvos and how to report back. The document then appears to have provided an example of how an order would be given. It states: "9 September 1995 neutralise C-40 with two salvos with the 4th MAP. "Report on the completed task." This language then appears to be translated into coded language as: "'CER,'" C-E-R, "'BARUT, 061, 072, 077, 078.'" This last part here is how this type of order would be conveyed in coded language to a subordinate unit; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is an example how an order would be conveyed and how these codes would be used. So the other side would have to have the same code table or list of code signs in order to be able to decipher the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And when you say "the other side," you mean the subordinate unit?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, the subordinate unit that the order is being sent to or rather who it is that one is communicating with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: According to this table, you would just substitute the word "BARUT" in this example with the word or phrase "Bedem 3A" if you wanted to strike this target with an aerial bomb; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't understand and I don't see that. Bedem, where is that? Let me just find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is on the previous page in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under the Jedinica, the units, we see that there is a number of units, the example related --

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- the example related to the 4th MAP, which is coded as BARUT, the aerial bomb, which appears to be a unit, is coded as Bedem 3A. You can just --

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You can just switch out those codes if you wanted an aerial bomb fired at this target; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And you mentioned it already, but in reports back to superior commands, units would confirm whether a task was completed; right? That was the practice.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Regular reports were sent, a regular daily combat report, during the course of the day. The situation, say, at 1700 hours, it was sent at 18- 1900 hours, I don't remember exactly. So it was a regular combat report where the situation in the units would be described. That is to say, over the past 24 hours and --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to go through and talk about reporting in some more detail. I was just asking if that was the practice, to report back if a task was completed; right? That's all I was asking you.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: If the task was received through such an order, that is to say directly by telephone, radio communication, et cetera; that is to say, using this code table, and then the code is written here. So then a report should be provided once the order had been carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 5 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, the codes 061 and following is not entirely clear to me yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I can go back to page 7 if that's -- if you want to look at that further, Your Honours. The numbers appear on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I think I now understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So there is corresponding numbers to the different aspects of that example. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, do I read this list correctly, that if you want to carry out actions per, you'd start it with the number 061? Do you see that on the table?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I also believe the other numbers that are in the example are also present in the list. I don't know if Your Honours want me to go through all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, I don't have to go through all of them, but I do see that there is always with the numbers 062 up to 074, there is always a corresponding C number. But for 061 it says -- it only says "Carry out actions per." I do not fully understand yet what distinguishes 061 from the other numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Maybe if I could give a quick attempt at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would just -- I just said it's not clear to me yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if you wanted to carry out actions against the target, you would -- there would be an order given that would be "carry out actions per" and then it would list the number of the target. Do I understand that right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, 061. That is to say, when the code 061 is presented during the conversation, this indicates the activity that should be carried out; that is to say, carry out whatever. So whoever receives the order writes 061 and then refers to the code - that is to say, the activity that should be carried out. 061, "fire at," et cetera. Now, within that point, there are several targets from one to the other, and then 062 or 070, 074, and then it indicates the target that should be engaged. May I go on explaining?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I now understand what it is. 061 stands for "take action." The following numbers, 62 to 74, stand for targets, and then, for example, 77 indicates how many salvos should be fired, and then reporting back is covered by 078. Is that well understood? I see your nodding "yes." That's then hereby on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I can now go to page 5 for the -- just to look at the associated tables to this -- to what we just looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So here we see that there is a list of co-ordinates for UNPROFOR on Igman, and we then see the C designations that correspond to the list that we just looked at. And then a bunch of co-ordinates. This is what the subordinate units would have to indicate if they got the code -- the example that was used was C-40, they would then use these co-ordinates to then target that location; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Aside from this type of targeting, just in general, artillery and mortar units in the SRK used pre-recorded targets from their previous firing missions; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: Otherwise, according to the rules, artillery units have to plan fire in advance. And fire is planned, target is planned in far greater numbers than will actually be realised in all combat activities. Every target is entered once activity is recorded. Say the enemy artillery fires, the observation post observes that, et cetera, but then we enter that target on a map and then we set the co-ordinates. We give these co-ordinates to the units in order for them to prepare in a timely fashion. So if that target starts firing, if it is the enemy artillery that is involved, we already have prepared co-ordinates and prepared elements for that target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The simple answer to the question therefore is, yes, the targets were prerecorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender 65 ter 32536 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a digression. I apologise. I did not see. For which period is this and what is the position of the Prosecutor on this code table?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the Prosecution has not taken any position yet. And if you think it would be interesting to know, then you can ask in re-examination the witness whether he has any knowledge about the time-frame for these tables. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 32536 receives number P7402.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 32535 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Colonel Simic, coming up before you is an SRK command order dated 19 September 1993. It's from Dragomir Milosevic after Operation Lukavac 93, one of the operations you discuss in your statement. The order is sent to all brigades. And, according to this order, the code tables, table signals, and other documents related to cryptographic communications must be destroyed. The documents used for coded communications were destroyed after operations or the lapse of a certain period of time; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC
utterances.text: That is the rule in peacetime and in wartime. Whatever is not being used should be destroyed. Because often the keys would be changed for the code tables, maps, et cetera. It changed often so that one and the same code names would not be used throughout the war. So then I don't know what the period involved was. Was it a month or two or three. For a certain operation they are used and then afterwards a commission destroys this and a record is written up on that, and then new code names are received and also keys, passwords for coded maps, and so on and so forth. That is the rule in peacetime and in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender 32535 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document receives number P7403.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not know if this would be a good time for the break. I'm going to go into something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a good time for the break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and will resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber was informed there were a few preliminary matters to be dealt with. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There was no precisely good time to deal with those, so we thought we'd deal with them forthwith. Three quick matters, the first two of which can be handled in public session, the last of which will require private session. The first concerns an imminent filing about which we wish to alert the Trial Chamber and have alerted the Defence. The backdrop to that filing was our February 2014 filing indicating the Prosecution's intention to annex a proof of death and injury chart or charts to the final brief and subsequent encouragement by the Trial Chamber to do so during the pendency of the case, if possible, with the understanding that the final annex to the final brief would supersede that temporary document, if necessary, but would still permit the parties and the Chamber the benefit of its use during the course of the case. Accordingly, we will be filing that this week. Secondly, as the Trial Chamber may have already have noted, we have filed our anticipated schedule for the Prosecution reopening to commence on the 22nd of June.
